text.title: Constitution Failure Modes
text.summary: Six ways a constitution dies. F1 is the one this methodology cannot prevent and must therefore state first: structure is checkable, meaning is not.

failure.symptom: The file validates, ships, and the code does whatever it did before. Nobody has cited a rule id in a review in months.
failure.cause: Semantic enforcement was assumed. The validator checks count, cap, why present, ids, sections and footer — it cannot check whether the codebase obeys `R-05`, and no static analysis can, because the rules are written in English about intent.
failure.prevention: State the limit rather than working around it: the Compliance section names the human or agent that reads the diff against the rules, and separates the rules a machine checks today from the ones only a reader checks. A constitution whose Compliance section says "everyone follows it" is already dead and has not noticed.

failure.symptom: Phases start loading "the relevant part" of the constitution, or stop loading it entirely and cite it from memory.
failure.cause: The cap was raised instead of forcing a merge, a demotion or a retirement. Every individual addition looked reasonable.
failure.prevention: Treat reaching twenty as the signal to remove something. Selective loading is the failure, not the workaround: rules that are loaded selectively apply selectively, and nobody can predict which ones were in context when a decision was made.

failure.symptom: The constitution contains table names, pricing tiers, API field shapes or the deploy topology. It is edited every sprint and its diff is unreviewable.
failure.cause: There was no second file to delegate to, or there was one and nobody pointed at it, so the constitution became the only place that felt authoritative.
failure.prevention: Name the `project-spec/` location in Scope on day one, even while the folder is nearly empty. Domain facts change on a different clock from working agreements; mixing them means the stable half inherits the volatile half's churn.

failure.symptom: Rules read "write tests", "keep code clean", "document decisions". Nobody objects to any of them and nothing changes.
failure.cause: The admission test was skipped, usually because the file had to exist before anyone knew what to put in it — a gate demanded a constitution, so a constitution was produced.
failure.prevention: Contestability is the part that does the work: if no competent engineer would choose otherwise, the rule carries no information and costs context on every load. A short constitution of five real rules beats twenty pieces of consensus.

failure.symptom: Two rules in the same file point in opposite directions. Whichever one supports the current argument gets cited.
failure.cause: The constitution was treated as a decision log: a changed position was appended below the old one instead of amending it, because deleting a rule felt like losing history.
failure.prevention: History belongs in `decisions.md` and ADRs, which are append-only and never pruned. The constitution is the standing set: amend or retire, bump the version, record the transition in the Sync Impact Report. Nothing is lost — it moves to the file built to hold it.

failure.symptom: Every rule has a why, and every why is a restatement of the rule. Exceptions get granted freely because nobody can weigh what would be lost.
failure.cause: The rules were drafted first and the reasons backfilled to satisfy the format. A backfilled why rationalises whatever was already decided and excludes nothing.
failure.prevention: Elicit the why first — "what have you had to explain twice?" — and write the rule from it. The test is whether the why alone rules anything out. If it does not, there is no rule there yet.
